item.title: An entropy-adjusted invariant likelihood for incidental parameters
item.description: arXiv:2611.31707v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Incidental parameters can make maximum likelihood inconsistent in short panels. When they act through a known translation group, integration with respect to Haar measure eliminates them exactly and gives an invariant likelihood, whose score is shown to be the conditional expectation, given the maximal invariant, of the Neyman-orthogonalised score of every order. Under interactive fixed effects the orbit is an unknown factor space, and the invariant score for it has a drift equal to minus the derivative of the entropy of the retained contrasts. An entropy adjustment removes this drift and, at the true structural parameter, identifies the factor space uniquely when the loadings span it. The adjusted estimating equations are the gradient of a single criterion if and only if the entropy separates into an orbit term and an error-law term, as in scale and elliptical families; consistency then follows from a design condition, and in general from an equilibrium-identification condition, with asymptotic normality for fixed panel length. A boundary is derived for recovering a skewness sign discarded by a two-period invariant reduction. An application to Vietnamese rice farming rejects equal household-effect weights across survey waves and finds lower returns to scale.
item.dc:creator: Xibin Zhang

item.title: Pragmatic Deeply Debiased ML
item.description: arXiv:2611.33069v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Debiased machine learning (DML) combines a fitted outcome regression with weighted residuals to remove first-order regularization bias when estimating parameters such as average treatment effects, yet a second-order bias remains whenever regression and weighting errors align. For linear regression functionals, we target this second-order bias by training a strong learner to predict first-stage residuals from many covariates, yielding a one-dimensional (or low-dimensional) working model whose bias contribution is estimated on an independent sample. To complement this targeted search, we also analyze general kernel-based corrections, including covariate partitions and smoothers. We prove that deeply debiased ML is algebraically identical to ordinary DML evaluated with a post-hoc regression update that adjusts each scored observation using kernel-weighted residuals from the remaining evaluation observations. In our empirical and simulation studies, strong initial DML learners often leave the second-order correction small relative to sampling uncertainty, in which case the correction serves as a diagnostic check alongside sensitivity bounds for any remaining misspecification bias.
item.dc:creator: Victor Chernozhukov, Chengchun Shi

item.title: Inference for Fixed Effects Estimators when Panels are Unbalanced
item.description: arXiv:2607.10246v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop the asymptotic theory for two-way fixed effects M-estimators in unbalanced panels, within a framework where both panel dimensions grow large at proportional rates. The selection process may be deterministic, stochastic, or a combination of the two. We require neither a missing-at-random condition nor a selection equation, only a conditional mean restriction on the outcome. The uncorrected estimators are asymptotically normal but not correctly centred due to incidental parameter bias and feedback bias. The latter can arise when regressors or the selection indicator respond to past outcomes. We propose debiased estimators that remove both biases without requiring knowledge of which regressors or selection components are predetermined. Simulations show that the corrections remove most of the bias and restore coverage close to nominal levels. Revisiting a study on capital inflow surges and banking crises, we find that the corrections leave qualitative conclusions unchanged but appreciably shift the estimated magnitudes.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Czarnowske, Amrei Stammann

item.title: Robust Signal Maximization in Spillover Experiments
item.description: arXiv:2607.18601v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the optimal design and analysis of experiments for estimating spillover effects. Assuming a linear exposure model, we characterize the treatment-assignment distribution and regression-based estimator that minimize worst-case approximate variance against a broad class of distributions of unobservables. The design problem yields an intuitive solution in which the planner trades off spillover signal strength against dispersion of spillover variation. The analysis problem yields a simple recentered instrumental variable estimator. We illustrate these new tools in semi-synthetic experiments based on three applications from development economics. Our approach yields large variance reductions, increasing effective sample sizes by 44-266%.
item.dc:creator: Kirill Borusyak, Peter Hull, Evan Munro

item.title: Flexible Matrix Estimation with Side Information
item.description: arXiv:2603.24833v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We introduce a flexible framework for high-dimensional matrix estimation to incorporate side information for both rows and columns. Existing approaches, such as inductive matrix completion, often impose restrictive structure---for example, an exact low-rank covariate interaction term, linear covariate effects, and limited ability to exploit components explained only by one side (row or column) or by neither---and frequently omit an explicit noise component. To address these limitations, we propose to decompose the underlying matrix as the sum of four complementary components: (possibly nonlinear) interaction between row and column characteristics; row characteristic-driven component, column characteristic-driven component, and residual low-rank structure unexplained by observed characteristics. By combining sieve-based projection with nuclear-norm penalization, each component can be estimated separately and these estimated components can then be aggregated to yield a final estimate. We derive Frobenius- and entrywise-norm convergence rates that demonstrate the robustness of our estimator across a broad range of model configurations with varying degrees of informativeness in the side information. We further extend the method to partially observed matrices under both missing-at-random and missing-not-at-random mechanisms, including block-missing patterns motivated by causal panel data. Simulations and a real-data application to tobacco sales show that leveraging side information improves imputation accuracy and can enhance treatment-effect estimation relative to standard low-rank and spectral-based alternatives.
item.dc:creator: Anish Agarwal, Jungjun Choi, Ming Yuan

item.title: Beyond Point Forecasts: A Survey on Probabilistic Forecasting for Time Series and Spatiotemporal Data
item.description: arXiv:2609.13345v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Probabilistic forecasting is central to decision-making under uncertainty, yet its methodological landscape has become increasingly fragmented across temporal and spatiotemporal forecasting, statistical modeling, machine learning, and deep generative modeling. This survey develops a unified perspective by organizing probabilistic forecasting methods according to where and how uncertainty is introduced into the forecasting pipeline. Our taxonomy connects model-agnostic approaches including ensembles and distribution-free calibration, with model-intrinsic approaches spanning Bayesian modeling, parametric predictive distributions, distributional regression, and modern generative models, and further examines the emerging role of time series foundation models. Beyond methodological synthesis, we identify the assumptions, computational demands, and forms of uncertainty represented by different paradigms, and translate these distinctions into data-driven and domain-specific guidance for method selection. We complement the survey with a cross-paradigm empirical study on univariate, multivariate, and spatiotemporal forecasting tasks. The results reveal that no single uncertainty-quantification paradigm dominates across settings. Calibration, sharpness, predictive accuracy, and computational efficiency can lead to substantially different model preferences, while expressive generative models and zero-shot foundation models exhibit markedly different accuracy-efficiency trade-offs. Lastly, we identify unresolved challenges surrounding uncertainty in evolving dependency structures, physics-informed predictive distributions, forecasting extreme events, handling count-valued, directional, and continuous-time series, and the development of unified software resources. Our survey provides both a conceptual framework and a practical roadmap for probabilistic forecasting research.

item.title: An adaptive $L_2$-type test for high-dimensional white noise
item.description: arXiv:2609.33418v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We propose a new $L_2$-type test for white noise which allows the dimension $p$ of the time series to either (i) be a fixed constant, or (ii) diverge with the sample size $n$. The proposed test statistic exhibits an interesting phase transition, following two different regimes of behavior: $p$ is fixed, and $p\rightarrow\infty$. Because identification of the operable regime is difficult, if not impossible in practice, we devise a novel adaptive bootstrap method to construct a unified testing procedure across different phases. Numerical experiments confirm the good finite sample performance of the proposed adaptive $L_2$-type test in comparison to the existing methods in the literature. The proposed testing procedure has been implemented in R package HDTSA.
item.dc:creator: Jinyuan Chang, Jing He, Weiming Li, Chen Lin

item.title: Announced Breaks Separate Conformal Reliability from Frequency Calibration
item.description: arXiv:2610.23917v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A prediction interval should contain the outcome at a stated rate. Conformal prediction sets its width from past forecast errors. When the process behind a time series changes on an announced date, intervals set from errors before that break can stop covering. After Australia moved to five minute electricity settlement, a 90% interval fixed beforehand covered 51.5% of the next 400 days. One forecaster needs the next interval to cover, another a finished period's share of misses at 10%. We show that each need calls for its own restart at the date. We recompute the next interval from the $n$ errors since the break. If these errors are independent, its coverage comes within $O(n^{-1/2})$ of the stated rate, the best order attainable. For a finished period, we restart adaptive conformal inference (ACI). On bounded errors, if a floor under its width adds a bounded total, it brings the share of misses within $O(n^{-1})$ of target but promises nothing about the next interval. After a simulated mean shift of 5.0 noise standard deviations, recomputed intervals cover within 3.5 percentage points of 90% on average at the 50th forecast, a third closer than the 5.2 of the best of five baselines. Of nine announced breaks in power markets and at a central bank, restarting ACI gives a detectable gain only at the one large break.
item.dc:creator: Karl Li
